name: Quetiapine (Seroquel)
summary: Second-generation antipsychotic used for bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and as an add-on for major depression. Often causes sedation and weight gain; can affect blood sugar, cholesterol, and heart rhythm—especially at higher doses or with other risk factors.
description: Quetiapine (Seroquel) is an atypical antipsychotic that can stabilize mood, reduce psychotic symptoms, and (at lower doses) help with sleep and anxiety in some people. It can be very sedating and is known for metabolic side effects like weight gain, higher triglycerides, and increased blood sugar. It can also cause orthostatic dizziness and, rarely, QTc prolongation—so dosing and monitoring matter. It is not approved for dementia-related psychosis due to increased mortality risk in older adults.
patient_summary: Quetiapine (Seroquel) can help with bipolar mood episodes, schizophrenia symptoms, and can be added to antidepressants for major depression. It can also be used off-label for anxiety or insomnia in select cases. Biggest tradeoffs: sleepiness, dizziness/low blood pressure, and metabolic changes (weight, cholesterol, blood sugar). It is not approved for dementia-related psychosis because antipsychotics increase death risk in that group.

primary_indications: Bipolar I Disorder (acute mania; bipolar depression; maintenance as monotherapy or adjunct depending on formulation/plan)
Major Depressive Disorder (adjunctive therapy; XR labeled)

linked_conditions.context: Used to reduce hallucinations, delusions, disorganization, and agitation; titration is usually gradual to balance symptom control with sedation and orthostatic side effects.
Used across bipolar illness: acute mania/mixed features (higher doses) and bipolar depression (often a bedtime-target dose).
Used as an add-on when antidepressants alone aren’t enough; XR is a labeled option for adjunctive treatment.
Sometimes used in refractory cases as monotherapy or add-on, usually in specialist settings because of sedation and metabolic risks.
Sometimes used for insomnia when there is a clear psychiatric comorbidity (like bipolar disorder or severe anxiety) and other options aren’t a fit.
May be used as an alternative agent for sleep, hyperarousal, or severe agitation, typically as adjunct to first-line therapies.
May be used as augmentation in treatment-resistant OCD, usually as add-on to an SSRI/SNRI or clomipramine under specialty care.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to quetiapine or any component of the formulation

efficacy_response.metric: Time to initial symptom improvement (varies by condition)
efficacy_response.patient_text: Quetiapine can start helping within days for agitation/mania in some people, within about a week for bipolar depression or as add-on for depression, and over 1–6 weeks for schizophrenia symptoms depending on the target and dose. The right question isn’t just “does it work,” but “does it work without causing too much sedation, metabolic change, or dizziness.”

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapidly absorbed orally; XR exposure increases with high-fat meals; light meals (~300 calories) have minimal effect on XR exposure
pharmacokinetics.onset: Condition-dependent; sedation can be felt quickly, while mood/psychosis benefits typically build over days to weeks
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Immediate release: ~1.5 hours; Extended release: ~6 hours
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Quetiapine: ~6–7 hours (adults); active metabolite norquetiapine: ~12 hours
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic via CYP3A4; forms active metabolite norquetiapine and inactive metabolites
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (~73% as metabolites; <1% unchanged) and feces (~20%)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: IR with food increases peak and AUC modestly; XR with high-fat meals increases exposure; XR should be taken without food or with a light meal (≤300 calories)

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Quetiapine (Seroquel) is used in psychiatry for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and it can be used as an add-on for major depression when antidepressants aren’t enough. Clinically, it’s also sometimes used off-label for severe anxiety or insomnia—but that’s usually reserved for situations where the psychiatric context makes sense and the benefits outweigh the very real tradeoffs (sedation, metabolic effects, dizziness).
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Helps reduce hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, and agitation
{link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar disorder}: Acute mania/mixed episodes, bipolar depression, and maintenance depending on the plan and formulation
{link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major depression (MDD)}: Add-on treatment (especially XR) when an antidepressant alone isn’t doing the job
off_label: Insomnia when there’s a clear psychiatric comorbidity (not as a first-choice sleep med)
ICU delirium-related agitation (short-term adjunct when needed)
Parkinson disease psychosis (low-dose strategy under specialist guidance)
Severe agitation/aggression with dementia (short-term adjunct only; high-risk population; not approved)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Quetiapine can feel wildly different depending on dose and what you’re treating (sleep/anxiety vs mood/psychosis). Here’s what people commonly describe:

quotes: It helped me sleep… but it also hit me like a truck.
I felt calm, heavy, and kind of glued to the couch.
Great for sleep—bad for getting out of bed the next day.
items.note: Sedation can be immediate and dose-related. Some people adapt over time; some don’t.

quotes: The edge came off my mania within a few days.
My mood stopped swinging so hard, but I felt slowed down.
It helped the depression, but I had to fight the daytime sleepiness.
My body finally relaxed, like my nervous system unclenched.
It lowered the intensity, but I felt kind of foggy.
It helped when I was spiraling, but I couldn’t take it if I had plans.
items.note: When used for anxiety/agitation, the benefit is often tied to calming/sedation—so the tradeoff is functioning.

quotes: I got hungry in a way I didn’t recognize.
I gained weight fast and my labs changed.
Standing up too fast made me feel like I’d black out.
items.note: Weight gain, lipid/glucose changes, and orthostatic dizziness are common reasons people stop.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Quetiapine has two timelines: sedation can show up fast, while the real psychiatric benefits typically build over days to weeks depending on what you’re treating and the dose you’re using.
key_points: Hours to first doses: Sedation and dizziness can show up quickly (especially at bedtime dosing)
Days: Mania/agitation may start improving within days for some people as doses ramp
~1 week: Bipolar depression or depression augmentation can show early improvement for some, with continued gains over weeks
1–2 weeks: Schizophrenia symptoms may start improving, with fuller response often taking 4–6 weeks
Half-life: Quetiapine ~6–7 hours; active metabolite norquetiapine ~12 hours (helps explain why effects can carry into the next day for some people)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Symptom response depends on diagnosis and dose
sections.text: Quetiapine is a core medication in several psychiatric conditions: schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (including bipolar depression), and it’s also used as an add-on option for major depression. Off-label, it may help anxiety or insomnia in select cases—but the benefit often comes from sedation, and that’s not free. The goal is symptom relief with tolerable side effects: stable mood without metabolic harm, psychosis control without disabling daytime sedation, and sleep help without turning the next day into a fog.
sections.clinical_details: Clinical response is typically evaluated by target symptoms (psychosis, mania, depression, agitation, sleep) and functional outcomes (work/school performance, relationships, self-care), while tracking adverse effects closely (weight, glucose, lipids, orthostasis, QTc risk, EPS/akathisia, and rare syndromes like NMS).

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Not approved for dementia-related psychosis. Antipsychotics increase mortality risk in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.
sections.black_box: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. Quetiapine is not approved for the treatment of patients with dementia-related psychosis. Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies. Monitor closely for clinical worsening and emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors, especially during the first weeks and after dose changes.
other: Suicidality monitoring: Watch closely in children, adolescents, and young adults when used in depression contexts; counsel families/caregivers to monitor and communicate changes
Sedation and falls: Can impair alertness and coordination; higher fall/fracture risk in older adults
Orthostatic hypotension and syncope: Especially during initiation or rapid titration
Metabolic effects: Weight gain, triglycerides and cholesterol changes, hyperglycemia/new-onset diabetes; rare severe hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis reported
QTc prolongation: Dose-related risk in susceptible patients; avoid or be cautious with QT-prolonging meds, electrolyte issues, or baseline prolonged QTc
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare): Medical emergency—fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability
Tardive dyskinesia/EPS: Lower risk than many antipsychotics, but not zero—risk rises with dose, duration, and vulnerability
Blood dyscrasias (rare): Leukopenia/neutropenia/thrombocytopenia reported; higher concern with low baseline counts or history
Catatonia: Antipsychotics aren’t indicated for catatonia and may worsen outcomes; specialist input is essential
Hepatic impairment: Clearance reduced; start low and titrate slowly; avoid in severe cirrhosis (high risk)
patient_counseling: If you’re over 65 with dementia-related psychosis, this medication is not approved and carries increased death risk—this is a big deal and should trigger a serious risk/benefit discussion.
Expect sleepiness and dizziness early on—don’t drive or operate machinery until you know how you react.
Stand up slowly. If you’re getting lightheaded or faint, tell your prescriber—dose and titration speed matter.
Track weight and appetite. If hunger ramps up, that’s not “in your head”—it’s a known effect.
Ask about baseline labs (glucose/A1c, lipids) and follow-up timing before you start.
Report chest pounding, fainting, severe palpitations, or anything that feels like an abnormal rhythm—especially if you have heart risk factors.
If you develop high fever, severe stiffness, confusion, or severe sweating/shaking—get emergency care (possible NMS).
If mood worsens, agitation increases, or suicidal thoughts appear—contact your prescriber urgently. Families/caregivers should help monitor early in treatment.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common issues are sedation, dizziness/orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth/constipation, and metabolic changes (weight gain, lipids, glucose). Movement side effects can happen but are usually less prominent than with many other antipsychotics.
plain_language_list: Sleepiness or feeling sedated (especially early, and at night-dosed regimens)
Dizziness when standing up (orthostatic hypotension) and possible fainting
Changes in cholesterol/triglycerides and blood sugar
Brain fog or slowed thinking (especially if dose is too high for your goal)
Restlessness/akathisia or tremor (less common, but can be very uncomfortable)

common.incidence: 18% to 57% (reported ranges vary by study/population and dose)
common.patient_note: This is one of the most noticeable effects. It can be helpful if sleep is part of the problem—but if you’re using it for mood/psychosis and feel flattened or foggy, the dose/timing may need adjusting.

common.incidence: 2% to 7% in adults; higher rates reported in some older-adult data
common.patient_note: Lightheadedness is most common in the first days of starting or after dose increases. Hydration, slower titration, and reviewing other blood-pressure-lowering meds can help.

common.incidence: Up to 9% to 44% (varies by age group and reporting source)
common.patient_note: Dry mouth can be annoying and can increase dental risk. Water, sugar-free gum, and dental hygiene matter more than people think.

common.incidence: Weight gain reported 4% to 23% (significant gain possible over time)
common.patient_note: This can happen fast and can be dramatic for some people. If weight is climbing early, it’s worth intervening early (nutrition plan, activity, and sometimes medication strategy changes).

common.incidence: Triglycerides 8% to 28%; hypercholesterolemia 7% to 18%; hyperglycemia reported
common.patient_note: Even if you feel fine, labs can shift. That’s why baseline and follow-up monitoring is part of responsible prescribing.
Dose-related anticholinergic effects can contribute. Constipation can get severe if ignored—bring it up early so it’s manageable.

serious: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (class warning)
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare): fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability—EMERGENCY
Severe metabolic complications (rare but real): new-onset diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe hypertriglyceridemia, pancreatitis
QT prolongation and rare torsades de pointes (usually overdose or multiple risk factors): palpitations, syncope—urgent evaluation
Severe hypotension/syncope and falls, especially in older adults or during rapid titration
Blood dyscrasias (rare): leukopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia; higher concern with low baseline counts or prior history
Hepatotoxicity (rare severe injury): jaundice, dark urine, severe fatigue; stop and evaluate
Tardive dyskinesia (risk increases with duration and total exposure): abnormal involuntary movements
Temperature dysregulation (rare): heat stroke risk in heat/exertion; reported hypothermia cases

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Quetiapine is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4. Interactions and additive side effects (sedation, low blood pressure, QTc effects) are the big practical issues.

items.with: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (example: certain azole antifungals, some macrolides, some HIV meds)
items.risk: Higher quetiapine levels → more sedation, hypotension, and side effects; toxicity risk rises.
items.action: Avoid or use specialist-guided dose reduction and close monitoring. If a strong inhibitor is unavoidable, reassess whether quetiapine is the right choice.

items.with: CYP3A4 inducers (example: carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St. John’s Wort)
items.risk: Lower quetiapine levels → reduced efficacy and symptom breakthrough.
items.action: Avoid if possible. If used together, expect reduced effect and need for careful reassessment (and possibly an alternative medication strategy).

items.with: Other sedatives (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, sleep meds)
items.risk: Additive CNS depression → heavy sedation, impaired coordination, falls, and overdose risk (especially with opioids/alcohol).
items.action: Minimize combinations. Avoid alcohol. Use the lowest effective doses and reassess daytime functioning and safety.

items.risk: More orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, and fainting.
items.action: Go slow with titration, monitor orthostatics, and adjust the overall regimen if syncope/dizziness emerges.

items.risk: Higher QTc prolongation risk → rare but serious arrhythmias.
items.action: Review QT risk before starting and after major dose changes; correct electrolytes; consider ECG monitoring in higher-risk patients.

items.risk: Reports suggest increased quetiapine exposure and higher rates of blood count abnormalities in some cases.
items.action: Use thoughtfully, monitor side effects and CBC if clinically indicated, and reassess if excessive sedation or hematologic issues occur.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Quetiapine isn’t a “stop it suddenly” medication for most people—especially after long-term use. If you stop abruptly, you can get withdrawal-like symptoms and rebound insomnia/anxiety, and your underlying condition can flare. If you’re stopping because of a serious adverse effect, switching strategies may matter more than taper speed.
key_points: If you’ve been off quetiapine for more than a week, many patients need re-titration rather than jumping back to the old dose.
Withdrawal/rebound symptoms can include agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, irritability, restlessness, tremor, and return of psychosis or mood symptoms.
General approach: Gradual dose reduction over weeks to months, tailored to diagnosis, duration of treatment, relapse risk, and side effects.
In chronic psychotic or bipolar disorders, clinicians often plan a switch (cross-titration or overlap-and-taper) rather than a hard stop.
If stopping due to severe adverse effects (like suspected NMS, severe liver injury, serious arrhythmia risk), urgent medical guidance is required and the plan may differ.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Quetiapine dosing is highly diagnosis- and formulation-dependent. Lower doses are often used for sedation/sleep or anxiety-adjacent targets, while schizophrenia and acute mania typically require higher doses. Immediate-release (IR) can be divided 1–3 times daily; extended-release (XR) is usually once daily (often evening) and should be swallowed whole.

adult.schizophrenia_ir_initial: 50 mg/day PO in 1–2 divided doses (some first-episode or sensitive patients: 12.5 mg PO BID)
adult.schizophrenia_ir_titration: Increase by 25–50 mg increments every ≥2 days based on response/tolerability
adult.schizophrenia_xr_initial: 300 mg PO once daily in the evening (empty stomach or light meal ≤300 calories)
adult.schizophrenia_xr_titration: Increase by up to 300 mg/day every ≥1 day based on response/tolerability
adult.bipolar_mania_ir_initial: 100–200 mg PO once daily at bedtime or in 2 divided doses on day 1
adult.bipolar_mania_ir_titration: Increase by 100 mg/day until 400 mg/day by day 4; thereafter increase by ≤200 mg/day as needed
adult.bipolar_mania_ir_max: 800 mg/day PO (some specialist use higher in select cases, with higher risk tradeoffs)
adult.bipolar_mania_xr_initial: 300 mg PO once daily on day 1; 600 mg PO once daily on day 2
adult.bipolar_mania_xr_titration: Adjust based on response/tolerability after day 2
adult.bipolar_mania_xr_max: 800 mg PO once daily (some specialist use higher in select cases, with higher risk tradeoffs)
adult.bipolar_depression_bedtime_initial: 50 mg PO once daily at bedtime
adult.bipolar_depression_bedtime_titration: Increase to 100 mg at bedtime on day 2; then increase by 50–100 mg/day to target
adult.bipolar_depression_bedtime_target: 300 mg PO once daily at bedtime by day 4–7
adult.bipolar_depression_bedtime_max: 300 mg/day (higher doses sometimes used clinically for select patients, but evidence for added benefit above 300 mg is limited)
adult.mdd_adjunct_titration: Increase to 150 mg/day on day 3 (IR in 1–3 divided doses; XR once daily)
adult.mdd_adjunct_typical: 150–300 mg/day PO (IR in 1–3 divided doses; XR once daily)
adult.anxiety_initial: 25 mg (IR only) to 50 mg PO once daily
adult.anxiety_titration: Increase gradually every ≥7 days based on response/tolerability
adult.anxiety_typical: 50–200 mg/day PO (IR 1–3 times daily; XR once daily)
adult.sleep_initial: IR: 25–100 mg PO at bedtime; XR: 50 mg PO at bedtime
adult.sleep_titration: XR may increase to 150 mg at bedtime by as early as day 3 and 300 mg by as early as day 5 if needed and tolerated
adult.agitation_delirium_icu_initial: 50 mg PO BID; in sensitive patients, some experts start 12.5 mg PO BID or 25–50 mg PO at bedtime
adult.agitation_delirium_icu_titration: Increase in 100 mg/day increments at intervals ≥1 day based on response/tolerability (or slower in smaller increments for sensitive patients)
adult.dementia_agitation_psychosis_short_term_: Increase gradually (example: weekly) based on response/tolerability
adult.hepatic_cirrhosis_ir_initial: 25 mg PO once daily; increase in 25–50 mg increments based on response/tolerability (divide into 1–3 doses as needed)
adult.hepatic_cirrhosis_xr_initial: 50 mg PO once daily; increase by 50 mg/day until effective dose achieved (XR not recommended for initial dosing in quetiapine-naive cirrhosis patients)
adult.hepatic_severe: Avoid use in severe hepatic impairment (example: Child-Turcotte-Pugh class C)
adult.renal: No dosage adjustment needed for kidney impairment (including dialysis/CRRT scenarios in typical guidance)
adult.older_adults_general: Use lower end of adult dosing and titrate slowly; avoid for behavioral symptoms of dementia/delirium unless nonpharmacologic options failed and risk of harm is high

sections.simple_explanation: At lower doses, quetiapine often acts mainly as a strong sedating/calming agent (helpful for sleep but can cause next-day grogginess). For bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, doses are typically higher and titrated deliberately to balance symptom control with side effects. IR can be split across the day; XR is usually once daily and should be swallowed whole.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Quetiapine can be used during pregnancy and breastfeeding in selected situations, but the decision should be individualized. The big themes are: use the lowest effective dose, avoid unnecessary polypharmacy, and monitor metabolic risks closely. In older adults, the dementia-related psychosis mortality warning is central and should shape decision-making.
sections.pregnancy: Quetiapine crosses the placenta. Large-class data for atypical antipsychotics do not show a clear major increase in congenital malformations overall, but individual outcome data vary and the safest plan depends on the psychiatric risk of relapse. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can lead to newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, feeding issues, tone changes, respiratory distress, somnolence, tremor). Tapering late in pregnancy solely to reduce newborn symptoms is generally not recommended; instead, use the lowest effective dose and monitor. Quetiapine has meaningful metabolic risk; monitor for gestational diabetes as part of standard prenatal care.
sections.lactation: Quetiapine is present in breast milk, and published reports typically suggest very low relative infant doses. Breastfeeding is often considered acceptable when infant exposure is low, but infants should still be monitored for sedation, poor feeding, irritability, or developmental concerns—especially if premature, low birth weight, or if other sedatives are used. Use the lowest effective dose and avoid unnecessary medication combinations.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for use in pediatric patients younger than 10 years. For older pediatric patients, quetiapine may be used for specific severe psychiatric conditions in a comprehensive treatment program, with close monitoring for weight gain, metabolic effects, blood pressure changes, and movement side effects.
sections.geriatrics: High-risk medication in adults ≥65. Avoid for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic approaches failed and there is a risk of harm to self/others. If used, start low, titrate slowly, reassess often, and attempt deprescribing when appropriate. For labeled indications like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, use may be appropriate but requires careful monitoring for falls, orthostasis, sedation, metabolic changes, hyponatremia/SIADH, and QT risk.
sections.hepatic: Hepatic impairment reduces clearance and increases exposure. In cirrhosis, start very low (IR 25 mg once daily) and titrate gradually; avoid in severe cirrhosis when risk is high. Monitor liver biochemistries when clinically indicated; in cirrhosis, baseline and early follow-up labs are often recommended.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment is generally needed across degrees of kidney impairment; quetiapine is not significantly removed by dialysis.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Sedation and functional impairment: daytime sleepiness, reaction time, work/school performance; reassess after initiation and dose changes
Orthostatic vitals and fall risk: especially in older adults and during early titration; ask about dizziness, near-falls, fainting
Weight/BMI: baseline, early follow-up (weeks 8–12), then periodic monitoring; intervene early if rapid gain occurs
Metabolic labs: fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipid panel at baseline and follow-up (often around 3–4 months), then at least annually or more often if abnormal
Blood pressure and heart rate: monitor for tachycardia and BP changes; pediatric patients can show hypertension signals
Movement side effects: akathisia, parkinsonism, dystonia, and tardive dyskinesia; use a standardized scale periodically (and more often if high risk)
ECG/QTc monitoring: as clinically indicated—baseline if risk factors; recheck after major dose increases or adding QT-prolonging meds
CBC: as clinically indicated, especially if low baseline WBC/ANC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia
Liver function tests: baseline and follow-up when hepatic disease is present or if symptoms suggest liver injury; in cirrhosis, more structured monitoring early in treatment is often used
Thyroid labs (TSH/T4): if symptoms suggest thyroid changes or if clinically indicated
Mental status and safety: suicidality monitoring (especially in younger patients when used in depression contexts), worsening agitation, emerging mania, psychosis relapse signals
Hyponatremia/SIADH risk in older adults: consider sodium monitoring with initiation and dose adjustments in higher-risk patients

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Quetiapine comes in immediate-release (IR) tablets and extended-release (XR) tablets. XR is typically once daily (often evening) and must be swallowed whole—don’t crush, break, or chew it.
items: Immediate-release tablets (Seroquel / generic): 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg, 300 mg, 400 mg
Extended-release 24-hour tablets (Seroquel XR / generic): 50 mg, 150 mg, 200 mg, 300 mg, 400 mg

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic that works by blocking (antagonizing) several brain receptors. The core antipsychotic effect is thought to come from a mix of dopamine (D2) and serotonin (5-HT2) blockade. It also blocks histamine (H1) and alpha-1 receptors, which helps explain why it can cause heavy sedation and orthostatic dizziness. Its active metabolite (norquetiapine) has additional receptor effects that may contribute to mood and side effects (including more anticholinergic-type symptoms in some people).

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Quetiapine is a first-line or core option in bipolar disorder (including bipolar depression) and a standard option for schizophrenia. In major depression, it’s usually considered when a person has had an inadequate response to antidepressants alone (as an add-on). Off-label use for anxiety or insomnia can be reasonable in select cases—especially when there’s bipolar disorder or significant agitation in the picture—but it’s not a casual sleep med. If the main goal is sleep and the person doesn’t have a strong psychiatric indication, the metabolic and cardiovascular tradeoffs often outweigh the benefit.

seo.title: Quetiapine (Seroquel): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects, Weight Gain & Safety
seo.description: Quetiapine (Seroquel/Seroquel XR) for bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and depression add-on: dosing, sedation, weight gain, metabolic labs, QT risk, interactions, tapering, and special populations.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Quetiapine is used for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (mania and bipolar depression). It can also be used as an add-on for major depression when an antidepressant alone isn’t enough. Off-label, it’s sometimes used for anxiety or insomnia in select cases—usually when there’s a psychiatric reason that makes the risk/benefit make sense.

faqs.q: Why does Seroquel make people so sleepy?
faqs.a: Quetiapine strongly blocks histamine (H1) receptors, which can cause heavy sedation—especially at lower-to-moderate doses and early in treatment. For some people, that’s the point (sleep), but for others it becomes the reason they quit (daytime fog, oversleeping).

It’s not a controlled substance and it doesn’t cause the classic addiction pattern like benzodiazepines or opioids. But your body can adapt to it, and stopping abruptly can cause rebound insomnia, anxiety, agitation, and symptom return. So it’s not “no consequences”—it’s more “not a drug of abuse in the usual way.”

Yes, it can. Quetiapine is known for increasing appetite and causing weight gain in a meaningful number of people, and it can also worsen triglycerides, cholesterol, and blood sugar. This is why baseline and follow-up metabolic monitoring isn’t optional—it’s part of safe prescribing.

faqs.q: Can quetiapine raise blood sugar or cause diabetes?
faqs.a: It can raise blood sugar and increase the risk of new-onset diabetes in some people, especially with longer exposure and with other risk factors. Monitoring fasting glucose or HbA1c (and acting early if numbers change) is how you reduce harm.

faqs.q: Is quetiapine safe in older adults?
faqs.a: It depends on why it’s being used. In older adults with dementia-related psychosis, antipsychotics increase the risk of death and quetiapine is not approved for that use. For conditions like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, it may still be used in older adults—but usually at lower doses with slower titration and closer monitoring for falls, low blood pressure, sedation, and metabolic changes.

faqs.q: Does Seroquel prolong QT or cause heart rhythm problems?
faqs.a: Quetiapine has a dose-related QTc prolongation risk that’s usually modest but can become clinically important in people with risk factors (baseline QT prolongation, low potassium/magnesium, heart disease, interacting meds, overdose). If you’ve had fainting, palpitations, or you’re on QT-prolonging meds, ask about ECG monitoring.

faqs.q: Can I use Seroquel just for sleep?
faqs.a: Sometimes—but it’s not a casual sleep med. If you have bipolar disorder, severe anxiety, or another psychiatric condition where quetiapine is pulling double duty, sleep benefit may be part of the plan. If the only problem is insomnia, the metabolic and cardiovascular tradeoffs often outweigh the benefit, especially long-term.

faqs.q: How do I stop quetiapine safely?
faqs.a: Most people should taper rather than stopping abruptly—especially after long-term use. A gradual reduction helps avoid rebound insomnia/anxiety and lets you catch early relapse symptoms. If you’re stopping because of a serious adverse effect, the plan should be guided urgently by a clinician.

faqs.q: Is quetiapine safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: It can be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding when clinically indicated, but it should be individualized. In pregnancy, the big issues are relapse risk if you stop treatment and metabolic monitoring (including gestational diabetes screening as part of routine prenatal care). In breastfeeding, reported infant exposure is generally low, but infants should be monitored for sedation or feeding issues—especially if premature or if other sedatives are involved.
